a_predicate_defect_I_found_in_my_own_reh: The insurance the coordinator asked for was 'count the refs before and after and treat any change you did not cause as a finding'. My first implementation counted `find "$GITDIR/refs/remotes" -type f | wc -l`. Rehearsed against a local bare remote it printed `FINDING: refs/remotes went 1 -> 2` on a fetch that added nothing: `find -type f` sees LOOSE files only, so a ref moving from the packed-refs file to a loose file reads as a new ref. A predicate that cries wolf on re-packing is worse than none, because the finding it exists to report would be indistinguishable from its own noise. Replaced with a NAME SET from `for-each-ref`, comparing membership and reporting ADDED and GONE by name: it does not care whether a ref is packed, and it names the ref instead of implying one. In the real repo both methods happen to agree at 149 (nothing is packed there today) - which is exactly why the fixture, not the repo, is what exposed it.
my_first_drill_of_the_replacement_was_a_: Having replaced the predicate I drilled it by rewriting the driver's fetch line to a bare `git fetch origin` with a second branch waiting on the fixture remote, so a ref would arrive during the fetch. It reported nothing, and 'no finding' was the answer I wanted. The reason was not the predicate: my sed pattern was `git fetch origin main` while the real line reads `git -C "$WT" fetch origin main`, so the substitution matched nothing and I had re-run the UNMODIFIED script against itself. `diff` of the two drivers was empty - the control that caught it - and a manual bare fetch proved the fixture would indeed have shown the ref. Re-drilled with the correct pattern the predicate fires and names it: `FINDING: remote ref NAMES changed - added [refs/remotes/origin/other] gone []`, while the real explicit refspec on the same fixture stays silent. Both halves measured, which is the only form in which a 'silent' instrument means anything. This is the same genus as the needles in my notes: the drill must be a legal mutation whose whole output I read, and an unmutated subject answers a different question.

The ledger already carries one physical namespace under four spellings - `netns-4026531840` (93 tokens), `4026531840` (48+), `[4026531840]` and `net:[4026531840]`. resource_identities.net:4026531840|tcp|0.0.0.0|443: Destination identity, measured not inferred. The remote is read from the vehicle: `git remote -v` gives origin = https://github.com/CaptTymur/skipi-crewing.git for both fetch and push, i.e. HTTPS, hence port 443 and not the 22 of the ledger's SSH entry. Namespace `4026531840` is the network namespace INODE: `readlink /proc/self/ns/net` = net:[4026531840]. Written bare, matching the form the existing GitHub-443 entries use, so that my declaration can actually collide with them - my first draft wrote `netns-4026531840`, which the coordinator measured as colliding with nothing at all. The address slot is 0.0.0.0, the schema's 'honest broadest', and deliberately so: github.com resolved to 140.82.121.3 at 15:43Z by `getent ahostsv4`, but GitHub rotates its addresses and a pinned IP the fetch does not reach would be false precisely when it matters, hiding a collision instead of raising one. The DNS lookup was a local resolver query made while building this request; it changes no remote state and is not the stage's action.
